metadata.file_name: 49. Bernardo et al. (2022). Contrasting Profiles of Low-Performing Mathematics Students in Public and Private Schools in the Philippines: Insights from Machine Learning.pdf
metadata.title: Contrasting Profiles of Low-Performing Mathematics Students in Public and Private Schools in the Philippines: Insights from Machine Learning

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Philippines sample from PISA 2018, drawn via a two-stage stratified random sampling design (187 schools selected across 17 regions, then students sampled within schools). The authors report downloading the publicly released PISA 2018 database and constructing an analytic dataset by excluding variables with 100% missingness and removing students with more than 50% missing values. Missing questionnaire variables in the reduced dataset were imputed using k-nearest neighbors (k=7), followed by normalization of variables to [0,1] (except SCHLTYPE) and correlation-based feature condensation. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation; given the use of standard ML classifiers (e.g., Random Forest) and the absence of any weight-variable mention, weighting is likely omitted or not discussed, which may affect population-representativeness and uncertainty estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Philippines PISA 2018 student questionnaire and school questionnaire data. Excluded three variables with 100% missingness (ICTSCH, ICTHOME, ST225Q03HA) and excluded students with more than 50% missing values, reducing the sample to 7091 students. Imputed remaining missing values in the reduced dataset using k-nearest neighbor imputation with k=7. Defined the binary target using PVMATH1 (PV1MATH): students with PVMATH1 < 357.7 (below Level 1) were coded as 1 (poor performers) and those with PVMATH1 ≥ 357.7 (Levels 1–6) were coded as 0 (better performers). Then analyzed public and private school students separately using SCHLTYPE (private: SCHLTYPE=1 or 2; public: SCHLTYPE=3).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (Philippines) — private schools (SCHLTYPE=1/2), PV1MATH-based Level 1 threshold
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (best): Precision=0.69, Recall=0.61, F1=0.65, Accuracy=0.79; ROC-AUC reported in Figure 2 (exact AUC value not provided in text).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data for the Philippines private-school students, the study leveraged internet mobile-phone access (ST012Q05NA), expectations of completing a vocational degree (ST225Q05HA), metacognitive-like email-safety judgment (ST166Q02HA), parents’ occupational status (HISEI), and expected job at age 30 (BSMJ) to classify poor versus better mathematics performers based on PV1MATH. It found that the Random Forest achieved the highest validation accuracy (0.79) and that lower values on these resource/aspiration-related variables were associated with identifying poor performers (with SHAP indicating inverse relationships for the shared top features). This indicates that interventions for low-performing private-school students should prioritize reducing digital access and strengthening realistic postsecondary/occupational expectations, while also addressing students’ ability to handle misinformation in online contexts, though the results are predictive and not causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (Philippines) — public schools (SCHLTYPE=3), PV1MATH-based Level 1 threshold
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (best): Precision=0.81, Recall=0.78, F1=0.79, Accuracy=0.79; ROC-AUC reported in Figure 2 (exact AUC value not provided in text).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data for the Philippines public-school students, the study leveraged internet mobile-phone access (ST012Q05NA), expectations of completing a vocational degree (ST225Q05HA), email-safety judgment (ST166Q02HA), parents’ occupational status (HISEI), and mastery motivation (WORKMAST) to classify poor versus better mathematics performers based on PV1MATH. It found that the Random Forest achieved the highest validation accuracy (0.79) and that lower values on shared resource/aspiration/metacognitive-related variables were associated with identifying poor performers, alongside public-school-specific motivational and engagement indicators (e.g., WORKMAST and ATTLNACT). This indicates that public-school mathematics support should target motivational persistence and value of schooling, alongside addressing socioeconomic constraints and students’ vulnerability to misinformation, while recognizing that SHAP-based importance reflects prediction rather than causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses the Philippines sample from PISA 2018 and constructs a binary mathematics outcome from PV1MATH (PVMATH1): students below Level 1 (PVMATH1 < 357.7) are coded as poor performers and those at Level 1 or higher as better performers. After excluding variables with 100% missingness and removing students with >50% missing values, the authors impute remaining missing questionnaire data using k-nearest neighbors (k=7), normalize predictors, and then train separate classifiers for private and public schools using SCHLTYPE. Across both school types, Random Forest is selected as the best model via exhaustive hyperparameter search with five-fold cross-validation, reporting validation Precision/Recall/F1/Accuracy; for private schools Accuracy=0.79 (F1=0.65) and for public schools Accuracy=0.79 (F1=0.79). SHAP is used to rank influential predictors, highlighting shared resource/aspiration and email-safety judgment variables, plus school-type-specific motivational/engagement factors. Limitations include the lack of reported PISA sampling-weight usage and the fact that SHAP importance supports prediction, not causal inference.
